MOCK CLAT 10030 (ESSENTIAL)
ANSWER & EXPLANATIONS
English Language
1.	Answer: A
Reference Line: “A tomato crisp wouldn’t taste like tomato and a cheese crisp wouldn’t taste like
cheese unless paired with ‘the right blend of spices’.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) This option is correct because the passage shows that even familiar flavours
must be adapted to local culinary expectations. The same named flavour may need different spices
in different markets. Hence, Option (a) is the correct answer.
(b) This option is incorrect because the company is described as evasive about the spices. Local
research is not meant to make the process fully transparent. Hence, Option (b) is not the correct
answer.
(c) This option is incorrect because the passage does not show chef-led work being replaced. Chefs,
local research and packet design are shown as part of the process. Hence, Option (c) is not the
correct answer.
(d) This option is incorrect because the passage shows the opposite of using one fixed flavour.
Crisps are adapted to local appetites. Hence, Option (d) is not the correct answer.
2.	Answer: D
Reference Line: “Clifford’s ‘creative design kitchen’ is clean and clinical.” / “When a flavour is
made from scratch, Wood goes to chef Pat Clifford...”
Difficulty Level: Difficult
Explanation: (a) This option is incorrect because the process is not shown as purely spontaneous.
The clean and clinical kitchen suggests controlled work and testing. Hence, Option (a) is not the
correct answer.
(b) This option is incorrect because the passage does not treat home cooking as the main model. It
focuses on restaurant expertise and industrial flavour design. Hence, Option (b) is not the correct
answer.
(c) This option is incorrect because chefs are clearly part of the flavour-development process.
Clifford demonstrates and helps develop flavours. Hence, Option (c) is not the correct answer.
(d) This option is correct because Clifford’s chef background works within a controlled design
kitchen. The process combines culinary expertise with industrial experimentation. Hence, Option
(d) is the correct answer.
3.	Answer: B
Reference Line: “Despite traditionally being less adventurous with crisps, Spanish appetites
have changed recently thanks to younger generations being exposed to different crisps on their
travels (and on the internet).”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) This option is incorrect because the passage does not suggest that Spanish
consumers rejected traditional dishes. In fact, traditional dishes are recreated through crisp
flavours. Hence, Option (a) is not the correct answer.

(b) This option is correct because the passage shows that Spain was earlier less adventurous with
crisps, but younger consumers’ exposure through travel and the internet made the market more
open to newer flavours. Hence, Option (b) is the correct answer.
(c) This option is incorrect because the passage does not show a universal preference for foreign
flavours. It only shows that exposure to different crisps changed consumer openness. Hence,
Option (c) is not the correct answer.
(d) This option is incorrect because restaurant culture is not shown as declining. Rather, a
restaurant chef helps recreate traditional dishes for packaged snacks. Hence, Option (d) is not the
correct answer.
4.	Answer: A
Reference Line: “The company is evasive over email when asked what these spices are, but there
are clues on its packets.”
Difficulty Level: Easy
Explanation: (a) This option is correct because the passage says the company does not reveal
exact spices, but packet images offer clues. The secrecy is reduced only partly. Hence, Option (a) is
the correct answer.
(b) This option is incorrect because the packets do not disclose exact recipes. The company remains
evasive about the actual spices. Hence, Option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) This option is incorrect because packet imagery does not replace local research. The passage
presents both as different parts of flavour-making. Hence, Option (c) is not the correct answer.
(d) This option is incorrect because consumer curiosity is not shown as ending secrecy. The
author’s curiosity continues even after seeing packet clues. Hence, Option (d) is not the correct
answer.
5.	Answer: D
Reference Line: “When I get home and Google ‘seasoning house’, all it throws up is the title of a
2013 British horror film about an orphan who murders soldiers.”
Difficulty Level: Difficult
Explanation: (a) This option is incorrect because the anecdote does the opposite of normalising
seasoning houses. The search result makes them seem obscure and difficult to identify. Their
public visibility remains limited. Hence, Option (a) is not the correct answer.
(b) This option is incorrect because the author’s confusion is used deliberately for effect. It is not
presented as personal incompetence but as evidence of opacity. The humour strengthens the point
about secrecy. Hence, Option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) This option is incorrect because the anecdote does not resolve the mystery at all. The reader
still does not know how flavour houses convert dishes into seasonings. The final moment leaves
the process more obscure. Hence, Option (c) is not the correct answer.
(d) This option is correct because the failed Google search comically highlights how hidden the
industrial flavour process is. The horror-film result adds irony and absurdity. The ending
reinforces the secrecy behind familiar packaged tastes. Hence, Option (d) is the correct answer.

LAW PREP
— Tutorial—	MOCK CLAT 10030 : ANSWER & EXPLANATIONS
6.	Answer: D
Reference Line: “The company is evasive over email when asked what these spices are, but there
are clues on its packets.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) This option is incorrect because “equivocal” means unclear, doubtful, or open to
more than one interpretation. It is close to “evasive” in suggesting indirectness rather than
openness. Since it supports the same sense of avoidance, it cannot be the antonym. Hence, Option
(a) is not the correct answer.
(b) This option is incorrect because “oblique” means indirect or not straightforward. In the
passage, the company avoids giving a clear answer about the spices. Therefore, “oblique” reinforces
the meaning of “evasive” rather than opposing it. Hence, Option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) This option is incorrect because “reticent” means unwilling to speak freely or reveal
information. The company’s conduct in the passage is similarly marked by withholding details.
Thus, it is not opposite in meaning to “evasive.” Hence, Option (c) is not the correct answer.
(d) This option is correct because “forthright” means direct, frank, and open in expression. Since
“evasive” implies avoiding a clear or direct answer, “forthright” gives the most accurate opposite
meaning in context. Hence, Option (d) is the correct answer.
7.	Answer: C
Difficulty Level: Easy
Reference: "Marvin had said, 'I swear to God that I will sit for three hours a day at the desk
surrounded by books,' but he hadn't said anything about studying, so he wasn't really going back
on his word."
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. The passage never suggests that Marvin plans to
begin studying once the kentuki is connected. His attention remains fixed on establishing the
connection, making this an unsupported assumption.
B) Incorrect. Nothing in the passage indicates that Marvin believes his father's punishment has
expired. He is still complying with the requirement to remain at the desk for three hours.
C) Correct. Marvin distinguishes between the literal wording of his promise and his father's
intended expectation. Since he promised only to sit at the desk surrounded by books and never
expressly promised to study, he convinces himself that he has honoured his commitment. This
literal interpretation forms the basis of his self-justification.
D) Incorrect. Since Option C accurately reflects Marvin's reasoning, "None of the above" cannot be
the correct choice.
8.	Answer: B
Difficulty Level: Medium
Reference: "A week before, when his father had discovered Marvin's real grades..." and "...if his
father ever found the time to discover anything else about his son again."
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. Marvin repeatedly conceals his actions from his father
by secretly installing the kentuki and using an undisclosed savings account. Such behaviour
reflects secrecy rather than mutual trust or open communication.

LAW PREP
— Tutorial—	MOCK CLAT 10030 : ANSWER & EXPLANATIONS
B) Correct. The father supervises Marvin's academic performance by imposing a study schedule
after discovering his grades. However, Marvin believes his father lacks the time to notice other
aspects of his life, suggesting emotional distance despite parental oversight.
C) Incorrect. The relationship cannot be described as entirely indifferent. The father's reaction to
Marvin's grades demonstrates concern and involvement, even if that involvement appears limited
to discipline.
D) Incorrect. The passage directly contradicts this claim. Marvin believes it may take months
before his father notices the kentuki and even suspects that his father is unaware of the existence
of his mother's savings account.
9.	Answer: B
Difficulty Level: Easy
Reference: "...he hadn't said anything about studying, so he wasn't really going back on his
word."
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. The expression does not refer to forgetting a promise.
Marvin clearly remembers what he promised and consciously interprets it in a particular way.
B) Correct. The idiom "going back on one's word" means failing to keep or honour a promise.
Marvin argues that he has not broken his promise because he complied with its literal wording,
even if he ignored its intended purpose.
C) Incorrect. The phrase concerns keeping promises rather than misunderstanding instructions.
Marvin fully understands what his father expected but deliberately distinguishes expectation from
wording.
D) Incorrect. Changing one's opinion is unrelated to the idiom used in the passage. The issue is
whether Marvin has fulfilled his commitment.
10.	Answer: D
Difficulty Level: Hard
Reference: "...he hadn't said anything about studying..." and "Marvin had paid for the kentuki
connection using his mother's savings account."
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. Marvin's conduct is not presented as morally
principled. He secretly avoids studying, conceals his actions from his father, and accesses money
without permission, making this characterisation inconsistent with the passage.
B) Incorrect. Although Marvin's reasoning follows an internal logic, it cannot be described as
completely honest. His literal interpretation of the promise and secret financial actions
demonstrate deliberate deception rather than genuine integrity.
C) Incorrect. Marvin's actions are not impulsive or irrational. He carefully plans his behaviour,
anticipates his father's ignorance, and deliberately conceals his activities, showing calculated
rather than reckless decision-making.
D) Correct. Throughout the passage, Marvin constructs explanations that minimise his sense of
wrongdoing. He narrowly interprets his promise to avoid studying and secretly uses his deceased
mother's savings while convincing himself that these actions are acceptable. This reflects
calculated self-justification and opportunism.

LAW PREP
— Tutorial—	MOCK CLAT 10030 : ANSWER & EXPLANATIONS
11.	Answer: B
Difficulty Level: Medium
Reference: "...it would be months before his father caught on that he'd installed a kentuki on the
tablet..." and "Marvin had already used that account on other occasions, and he was starting to
suspect that not even his father knew it existed."
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. The passage suggests the exact opposite. Marvin
believes his father is unlikely to discover the kentuki for months, indicating minimal monitoring of
his digital activities.
B) Correct. Marvin intentionally hides both the installation of the kentuki and his use of his
mother's savings account. His confidence that these actions will remain undiscovered
demonstrates that secrecy is central to his plan.
C) Incorrect. At no point does Marvin express guilt or regret about purchasing the kentuki.
Instead, he appears excited about establishing the connection.
D) Incorrect. Since both Options A and C are unsupported by the passage, "All of the above"
cannot be correct.
12?	Answer: C
Difficulty Level: Hard
Reference: "...he hadn't said anything about studying, so he wasn't really going back on his
word." and "Marvin had paid for the kentuki connection using his mother's savings account... He
was starting to suspect that not even his father knew it existed."
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. Although Marvin's reasoning may appear subtly
amusing to readers, the passage is not celebratory. It centres on deception, secrecy, and strained
family dynamics rather than joy or humour.
B) Incorrect. The narration does not look back on past experiences with reflection or nostalgia.
Instead, it presents Marvin's present actions and thought process in a detached, immediate
manner.
C) Correct. The narration calmly presents Marvin's attempts to justify ethically questionable
behaviour without openly condemning him. This creates dramatic irony, as readers recognise the
flaws in his reasoning while Marvin believes he is acting fairly. Beneath this restrained narration
lies moral tension arising from deception, misuse of money, and emotional distance within the
family.
D) Incorrect. While the passage contains ethical conflict, it does not create an atmosphere of
tragedy or despair. The dominant effect is one of quiet irony and understated unease rather than
overwhelming sorrow.
13.	Answer: B
Difficulty Level: Easy
Reference: "I didn't ask you to leave... I didn't push you into the water, I didn't fetch you from
your village or field or ruin of a suburb and put you in your wretched leaky boat..."
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. The speaker's initial response is not sympathetic.
Instead of expressing compassion, she immediately emphasises that she did not cause the caller's
predicament, creating a defensive and emotionally distant tone.

LAW PREP
— Tutorial—	MOCK CLAT 10030 : ANSWER & EXPLANATIONS
B) Correct. The repeated statements beginning with "I didn't" demonstrate the speaker's
insistence that she bears no personal responsibility for the migrant's decision to undertake the
dangerous journey. This denial of responsibility dominates her immediate reaction.
C) Incorrect. The passage contains no promise of rescue. Although the speaker later explains the
practical limitations of rescue operations, she never assures the caller that help will arrive
immediately.
D) Incorrect. The speaker does not blame governments or authorities. Her remarks focus on her
own lack of responsibility and the overwhelming demands placed upon her rather than on the
causes of the crisis.
14.	Answer: A
Difficulty Level: Medium
Reference: "There are guys like you everywhere tonight, forty small boats supposedly sinking at
the same time in the Channel and I can't see to everyone at once."
Explanation for all options: A) Correct. Although the speaker initially sounds harsh and
emotionally detached, the later part of the passage reveals the immense pressure of responding to
numerous simultaneous emergencies. Her frustration arises from being overwhelmed by limited
capacity rather than from a complete absence of concern.
B) Incorrect. The passage contains no indication of calmness or optimism. The repeated references
to multiple sinking boats and the inability to help everyone convey stress and emotional strain.
C) Incorrect. While the speaker's language appears unsympathetic, she clearly recognises the
seriousness of the crisis. Her frustration stems from operational limitations, not complete
indifference to human suffering.
D) Incorrect. The passage never suggests that the speaker takes pride in refusing assistance.
Instead, her words reflect exhaustion and helplessness in the face of overwhelming demands.
15.	Answer: B
Difficulty Level: Easy
Reference: "So you'll just have to grin and bear it and let me get on with my job."
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. The idiom does not imply pretending to enjoy
suffering. It refers to enduring an unpleasant situation despite discomfort.
B) Correct. "Grin and bear it" means to tolerate hardship patiently without complaint. In the
passage, the speaker bluntly tells the caller to endure the situation while she attends to other
urgent responsibilities.
C) Incorrect. The phrase does not suggest ignoring danger. Rather, it encourages patient
endurance despite continuing hardship.
D) Incorrect. The idiom has no connection with laughing at one's own errors. Its meaning relates
to perseverance in difficult circumstances.
16.	Answer: C
Difficulty Level: Medium
Reference: "I didn't ask you to leave... I didn't push you into the water, I didn't fetch you from
your village or field or ruin of a suburb..."

LAW PREP
— Tutorial—	MOCK CLAT 10030 : ANSWER & EXPLANATIONS
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. A euphemism softens harsh or unpleasant ideas. The
speaker's language is direct and accusatory rather than softened or indirect.
B) Incorrect. Personification attributes human qualities to non-human entities. No such technique
is employed in the repeated clauses.
C) Correct. The repeated opening "I didn't" is a clear example of anaphora, a rhetorical device in
which successive clauses begin with the same words. This repetition reinforces the speaker's
persistent denial of personal responsibility and heightens the emotional intensity of the
monologue.
D) Incorrect. Although the passage contains vivid imagery elsewhere, this particular pattern is not
metaphorical. Its primary stylistic feature is repetition.
17.	Answer: B
Difficulty Level: Hard
Reference: "...forty small boats supposedly sinking at the same time in the Channel and I can't
see to everyone at once."
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. The passage explicitly rejects this assumption. The
speaker repeatedly states that she cannot respond to every emergency simultaneously because too
many boats require assistance.
B) Correct. The speaker's remarks rest on the practical reality that rescue resources are limited.
Because numerous emergencies occur at the same time, she must prioritise whom she can help
first. This operational constraint explains both her frustration and her defensive tone.
C) Incorrect. Although the speaker uses the word "supposedly," " she does not accuse the caller of
fabricating the emergency. Her concern lies with the sheer number of distress calls rather than
questioning the caller's honesty.
D) Incorrect. Since Option B accurately reflects the underlying assumption in the passage, "None
of the above" is incorrect.
18.	Answer: D
Difficulty Level: Hard
Reference: "I can't see to everyone at once."; "...forty small boats supposedly sinking at the same
time in the Channel..."; "...thirty at once on a raft that can scarcely take the weight of five, no
instruments, nothing to steer by..."
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. While the passage depicts the perilous conditions
faced by migrants, its central focus is not on celebrating their courage. Instead, it examines the
difficult position of the rescue operator confronted with overwhelming demands.
B) Incorrect. Although mobile phones are briefly mentioned, the passage does not criticise rescue
technology. The reference serves only to illustrate the scale of simultaneous distress calls rather
than to condemn technological tools.
C) Incorrect. References to the English Channel merely provide the setting for the events. The
passage does not aim to explain geographical features or maritime conditions.
D) Correct. The extract explores the ethical and operational dilemma faced by the speaker, who is
expected to respond compassionately while lacking the capacity to rescue everyone immediately.
The passage highlights the tension between humanitarian responsibility and practical limitations,
making this its dominant thematic purpose.

LAW PREP
— Tutorial—	MOCK CLAT 10030 : ANSWER & EXPLANATIONS
19.	Answer: B
Difficulty Level: Easy
Reference: "I recall most vividly the house itself, which struck me as an absolute mansion." and
"The visit impressed me terribly."
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. The narrator was not formally welcomed into the
family's private living spaces. Instead, his mother quietly took him into the house "by a side door,"
and they spent time only in the servants' quarters. This option contradicts the passage.
B) Correct. The narrator repeatedly emphasises the extraordinary impression made by Hundreds
Hall. Its scale, architecture, and ageing beauty appeared magnificent to a ten-year-old village
child, highlighting the contrast between the grandeur of the estate and his own ordinary
background. This explains why the memory remained so vivid.
C) Incorrect. The narrator explicitly states that his memory of the Ayres family is "vague" and that
he remembers "most vividly the house itself." Therefore, the house—not Colonel Ayres—forms the
centre of his recollection.
D) Incorrect. Since Option B is directly supported by the passage, "None of the above" is incorrect.
20.	Answer: A
Difficulty Level: Medium
Reference: "There were no trips inside, of course. The doors and French windows stood open, but
each had a rope or a ribbon tied across it." and "The lavatories set aside for our use were the
grooms' and the gardeners’, in the stable block."
Explanation for all options: A) Correct. Although the villagers were invited to attend the féte,
strict physical and social boundaries remained in place. Visitors were prevented from entering the
main house and directed to servants' facilities, demonstrating the rigid class distinctions that
governed access and privilege.
B) Incorrect. The passage explicitly states that entry into the mansion was restricted by ropes and
ribbons across the doors. Visitors were permitted to enjoy only the grounds, not unrestricted
access to the house.
C) Incorrect. The servants clearly occupy a subordinate social position. They perform demanding
household work while the Ayres family remains separate, indicating that they do not share the
family's privileges.
D) Incorrect. Nothing suggests that the narrator's family belonged to the aristocracy. On the
contrary, they attended the féte as village guests, and the narrator's mother entered through her
acquaintance with the servants rather than through social status.
21.	Answer: A
Difficulty Level: Medium
Reference: "They made it look blurred and slightly uncertain—like an ice, I thought, just
beginning to melt in the sun."
Explanation for all options: A) Correct. The simile conveys a sense of fading splendour.
Although Hundreds Hall still appears magnificent, its worn materials and softened appearance
suggest gradual decline and impermanence, much like melting ice slowly losing its shape.
B) Incorrect. The comparison is visual rather than literal. The narrator is not describing
temperature but the uncertain, fading appearance of the building.

C) Incorrect. The passage does not compare the colour of the house to ice. Instead, the comparison
focuses on its blurred outline and the impression of gradual dissolution.
D) Incorrect. There is no reference to fire or physical destruction. The imagery suggests slow decay
rather than sudden damage.
22.	Answer: B
Difficulty Level: Easy
Reference: "...like an ice, I thought, just beginning to melt in the sun."
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. Personification attributes human qualities to non-
human objects. The house is not given human characteristics in this comparison.
B) Correct. The comparison explicitly uses the word "like," making it a simile. By comparing the
house to melting ice, the narrator evokes fading beauty, fragility, and gradual decline.
C) Incorrect. Hyperbole involves deliberate exaggeration. The narrator is making an imaginative
comparison rather than exaggerating reality.
D) Incorrect. Irony depends on a contrast between expectation and reality. The quoted sentence
instead relies on figurative comparison to create imagery.
23.	Answer: C
Difficulty Level: Medium
Reference: "The girls had such a mountain of crockery to wash, my mother rolled up her sleeves
to help them."
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. Although the narrator vividly recalls the kitchen, he
expressly states, "I recall most vividly the house itself." Therefore, the mansion—not the servants'
quarters—made the strongest impression.
B) Incorrect. The passage directly contradicts this statement. Visitors were prevented from
entering the house, and ropes marked restricted areas, demonstrating that access remained
limited.
C) Correct. The passage explicitly states that the narrator's mother voluntarily assisted the
kitchen staff with washing dishes despite attending the féte as a guest. Her willingness to help is
directly supported by the text.
D) Incorrect. Since both Options A and B are contradicted by the passage, "All of the above" cannot
be correct.
24.	Answer: B
Difficulty Level: Hard
Reference: "I first saw Hundreds Hall when I was ten years old."; "I recall most vividly the house
itself, which struck me as an absolute mansion."; "The visit impressed me terribly."
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. The narrator does not express resentment or blame.
Instead, he recalls the experience with admiration and reflective warmth, making the tone
inconsistent with bitterness.
B) Correct. The passage recounts a childhood memory through vivid sensory detail and
affectionate recollection. Descriptions of the mansion, its architecture, and the excitement of
entering its hidden spaces create a nostalgic atmosphere infused with quiet wonder. Even the

subtle hints of the house's decline enhance the reflective quality of the narrative rather than
overshadowing it.
C) Incorrect. The passage contains neither satire nor comic exaggeration. The descriptions are
sincere and evocative rather than humorous or mocking.
D) Incorrect. Although the basement corridor is compared to a castle dungeon, the dominant mood
is not one of fear or suspense. The narrator experiences fascination and delight, particularly when
rewarded with the uneaten jellies, reinforcing the passage's nostalgic tone rather than creating
tension.
Current Affairs Including General Knowledge
25.	Answer: D
Difficulty Level: Easy
Reference: Founding members of the Pax Silica Initiative and India's subsequent accession to the
framework.
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. Australia was one of the original members of the Pax
Silica Initiative and participated in the founding coalition that sought to strengthen trusted AI,
semiconductor, and critical mineral supply chains.
B) Incorrect. Japan was a founding participant in Pax Silica and has played an important role in
advancing semiconductor cooperation and resilient technology supply chains among partner
nations.
C) Incorrect. Israel was included among the original founding members of the initiative, reflecting
its strategic importance in advanced technology and innovation ecosystems.
D) Correct. India was not a founding member of Pax Silica. Although absent from the inaugural
coalition, India formally joined the initiative later by signing the Pax Silica Declaration in
February 2026, thereby becoming part of the trusted technology partnership.
26.	Answer: C
Difficulty Level: Easy
Reference: India's accession to the Pax Silica Declaration (February 2026).
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. December 2025 marked the period of the inaugural
discussions and formation of the initiative, but India had not yet joined.
B) Incorrect. India did not become a formal participant in January 2026. No declaration was
signed during this period.
C) Correct. India officially became part of the Pax Silica framework by signing the Pax Silica
Declaration in February 2026, allowing it to participate in collaborative efforts relating to AI,
semiconductors, and resilient supply chains.
D) Incorrect. By April 2026, India was already a participating member. The formal accession had
taken place two months earlier.
27.	Answer: B
Difficulty Level: Medium
Reference: Strategic objective of Pax Silica to diversify AI, semiconductor, and critical mineral
supply chains.

Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. Pax Silica is an economic and technology-oriented
partnership rather than a military alliance. Its objectives are unrelated to NATO's defence
expansion.
B) Correct. The initiative seeks to reduce excessive dependence on China's dominance in critical
minerals, semiconductor manufacturing, and advanced technology supply chains by promoting
trusted and diversified international partnerships.
C) Incorrect. Pax Silica does not seek to counter European regulatory policies. In fact, the
European Union has become an active participant in the initiative.
D) Incorrect. Although energy security remains an important geopolitical issue, Pax Silica
primarily focuses on AI technologies, semiconductor ecosystems, and critical minerals rather than
Russia's energy exports.
28.	Answer: B
Difficulty Level: Medium
Reference: Status of participation in the Pax Silica Initiative (June 2026).
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. The number of participating countries had expanded
beyond 28 by June 2026 as additional nations endorsed the initiative.
B) Correct. As of June 2026, 35 nations, including the European Union as a bloc, had either signed
the Pax Silica Joint Declaration or endorsed its guiding principles, reflecting the initiative's
growing international acceptance.
C) Incorrect. The initiative had not yet reached participation from 42 nations by June 2026.
D) Incorrect. Participation had expanded considerably but had not reached 50 countries during the
stated period.
29.	Answer: A
Difficulty Level: Easy
Reference: Basic facts relating to the European Union.
Explanation for all options: A) Correct. Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The European Union
comprises 27 member states, and Brussels, Belgium, functions as its principal administrative and
institutional centre.
B) Incorrect. While Statement 2 is correct, Statement 3 is incorrect because not every EU member
has adopted the Euro. Several member states continue to use their national currencies.
C) Incorrect. Although Statement 1 is correct, Statement 3 is incorrect since the Euro is used only
by the members of the Eurozone, not by all EU countries.
D) Incorrect. Statement 3 is factually incorrect, making this option incorrect despite Statements 1
and 2 being accurate.
30.	Answer: C
Difficulty Level: Easy
Reference: Current leadership of the Indian Navy (June 2026).
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. General Upendra Dwivedi is the Chief of the Army
Staff and heads the Indian Army, not the Indian Navy.
B) Incorrect. Air Chief Marshal Amar Preet Singh is the Chief of the Air Staff and leads the Indian
Air Force rather than the Navy.

LAW PREP
— Tutorial—	MOCK CLAT 10030 : ANSWER & EXPLANATIONS
C) Correct. Admiral Krishna Swaminathan is the current Chief of the Naval Staff (CNS). As the
professional head of the Indian Navy, he oversees operational readiness, strategic planning, force
modernization, and maritime security.
D) Incorrect. Admiral Dinesh Kumar Tripathi served as the Chief of the Naval Staff before
Admiral Krishna Swaminathan and is no longer the incumbent.
31.	Answer: D
Difficulty Level: Easy
Reference: Tri-Commissioning of INS Dunagiri, INS Sanshodhak and INS Agray.
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Limited is India's
premier warship and submarine builder, but it did not construct the three vessels commissioned
during this event.
B) Incorrect. Cochin Shipyard Limited has built several major naval platforms, including aircraft
carriers, but it was not responsible for these three vessels.
C) Incorrect. Goa Shipyard Limited specializes in patrol vessels and other naval platforms;
however, it was not the shipyard involved in this tri-commissioning.
D) Correct. Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers (GRSE), Kolkata, built INS Dunagiri, INS
Sanshodhak, and INS Agray, demonstrating India's expanding indigenous shipbuilding capability.
32.	Answer: B
Difficulty Level: Medium
Reference: Project 17A of the Indian Navy.
Explanation for all options: A) Incorrect. Nuclear-powered attack submarines are being
developed under separate indigenous submarine programmes and are not part of Project 17A.
B) Correct. Project 17A is the Indian Navy's programme to construct seven advanced stealth
guided-missile frigates featuring enhanced stealth, modern sensors, vertical launch missile
systems, and high indigenous content.
C) Incorrect. Aircraft carriers constitute a separate class of capital warships and are not included
under Project 17A.
D) Incorrect. Hydrographic survey vessels serve a different operational role and are developed
under independent shipbuilding programmes.
33.	Answer: D
